text: That same night, just after twelve: ramen outside a convenience store, and Nib eating kimbap under his mask.
Then a pair of black boots, and a chair dragged right up against his.
The woman from behind the glass doors drops into it, far too close and perfectly at ease, with two canned coffees.
Jaeha goes red and plays dumb. Nib watches, a grain of rice stuck to his mask.
She doesn't let him. Han Sora, twenty-seven, Black Hound's crossbow. She was there at Gate 0912.
The blush is gone. He hasn't forgotten which side of that door she was on.
She's Mok's messenger, with one detail that matters: on Saturday, the hero goes in first, on camera.
The polite mask goes straight back on. It's the easiest promise he has ever made.
Then she turns her smile on Nib and goes fishing. Jaeha gives her a joke.
She leans closer with questions nobody asks about a doll, and gets straight-faced answers.
That gets a real laugh out of her.
The compass from the atrium hangs on her wrist, its violet needle pointing vaguely between Jaeha and Nib.
Four years of trap-testing taught him to ask what sets a thing off. What sets off this needle?
While she describes a drowned cathedral full of bells, Jaeha runs an experiment.
One tap on his knee sends the order down the link: one second of field form.
Across the table, Nib's eye flashes amber and goes out again, between one chew and the next.
The needle swings hard at Nib.
Then the amber is gone, and the needle drifts back to lean at Jaeha.
Sora glances at her wrist, surprised. Jaeha sips his coffee with a perfectly innocent face.
Experiment over. The needle only leans at him. What it hunts is a summon that's wide awake.
She leaves with a lazy salute and some advice that could be friendly, or a warning.
She walks off under the streetlamp, in no hurry at all.
Once she's gone, Nib says what that needle is made of. New rule: near her, both summons play dead.
Thursday morning, the roof is turning into a garden: Borro has planted lettuce all along the gutter.
Seoa negotiates like the household budget depends on it. Nib negotiates like a soldier who expects poison.
Nib folds at lightning speed, perfectly serious, while Seoa proves the crackers are safe.
That afternoon, Bomi isn't grinning. A streamer knows how to dig, and she's found something.
One entry stands out: a raid four years ago that killed a man Jaeha knows, officially by accident.
Jaeha goes very still.
Oh Minseok is the reason that notebook exists. And on his last night, Jaeha was with him.
Choi climbs up with kimbap and an old file, and for once he isn't smiling. Bomi made a call.
The Association's report on that night: a yellowed page, a stamp, a heavy signature.
It was Mok who wrote accident. Four years before he shut a door on Jaeha, he signed off on this one.
Bomi and Yerin gasp. Nib freezes with a shirt half folded. Jaeha doesn't move at all.
Then Choi sits down heavily with a confession of his own: he was the rescue worker that night, and he dragged a boy away.
Jaeha's cold face cracks. Choi has just described the worst night of his life.
And the colour drains out of the world.
Four years ago, in the Han River gate, an iron door grinds shut by itself. Two trap-testers run for the gap.
Minseok shoves twenty-year-old Jaeha through the gap and stays on the inside.
Through the last of the gap, he grins and gives Jaeha the rule Jaeha has lived by ever since.
The door slams. Jaeha hammers on the iron with both fists.
A younger Choi drags him away, the boy still screaming that someone is in there.
Above the door, a small lamp burns red. The same warning, four years earlier.
Back on the rooftop, Jaeha and Choi just look at each other.
Choi's report said the lamp was red, until someone took it out. Without it, Minseok's death is just an accident.
And Bomi has the one weapon Mok can't buy off: a camera, and an audience the size of a country.
Late that night, Jaeha sits alone under a bare bulb, while Nib sleeps curled in Borro's shell.
He turns back to the oldest pages, in handwriting that isn't his, carried for four years.
In one margin, a stick figure in a vest gives a thumbs-up.
Then a clean page, and the pencil pressing hard: a man, a mentor and a river, joined by lines.
His eyes are wet, and hard.
The notebook snaps shut.
At the parapet, he looks toward the river. The man who gave him his only rule broke it himself.
In Borro's shell, one yellow eye opens.
Nib comes to stand beside him. He knows about going first for someone, and being left behind.
And the scout nobody came back for has a suggestion for Saturday.
Far off across the roofs, under one pier of a bridge, a faint white-cyan glow.
Then his phone buzzes: a goodnight message, a reminder about Saturday, and a heart signed S.
Jaeha smiles, cold. Going first was always his job. On Saturday, it's his plan.
